scenarios.title: Bank the puck off the wall
scenarios.objective: Use a wall option to change the route around a defender, then read the rebound.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x). F1 owns the puck between the middle and the side boards. D1 is near the direct route to YOU, who are farther up ice and wider. F2 is closer to the middle; D2 is farther toward the right net. A bank off the side boards is one possible route to assess.
cues: D1 is near the direct passing route.
YOU are farther up ice and wider than D1.
F2 is closer to the middle; D2 may affect that option.

questions.prompt: Which defender is nearest the direct F1-to-YOU passing route?

options.text: D1
D2
Neither defender is near that route

questions.explanation: D1 is near the line between F1 and YOU. The freeze does not prove stick reach or an interception.

questions.prompt: Which two details matter before using the wall?

options.text: Where the rebound would leave YOU and D1
Whether the inside option to F2 stays clear of D2
That the wall sends the puck to the same spot every time

questions.explanation: The wall changes the route but not the need to read the rebound, pressure, and inside support.

questions.prompt: Arrange a wall-option plan.

options.text: See D1 and the wall space
Choose a reachable bank point
Read the rebound before the next touch

questions.explanation: The route around D1 is only useful if the rebound and next lane remain controllable.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the side boards, farther up ice than D1, to offer a possible bank-pass target.
questions.explanation: The example moves YOU closer to the side boards and farther up ice than D1. F1 still needs to judge a reachable bank point and rebound; no bounce or completed pass is guaranteed.

questions.prompt: D1 turns toward the boards before F1 releases. What should you revisit?

options.text: Whether the wall route or F2 lane is now more reachable
Bank the puck without looking because D1 moved
Pass through D1 to the original spot

questions.explanation: D1 turning toward the boards is a cue to reassess, not proof that a route closed or opened. Compare the bank option with F2 and D2 before choosing.

questions.prompt: How is a wall option different from simply passing through D1?
questions.explanation: It changes the puck route around the defender and creates a new rebound to read. The option remains conditional on the rebound and support.

scenarios.title: Open the shooting lane
scenarios.objective: Reassess a shooting lane when a defender moves toward another attacker.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x). YOU control the puck in the middle of the attacking zone; D1 is between YOU and the net. F2 is wider and farther toward the right goal line. If D1 moves, reassess both the shooting lane and the pass.
cues: D1 occupies the direct shooting line.
F2 is wider and closer to the right goal line than YOU.
The freeze does not prove a shot will reach the net or score.

questions.prompt: Who is between YOU and the right net?

options.text: F2
D1
The goalie only

questions.explanation: D1 is between YOU and the goalie in the direct lane.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should be read together?

options.text: D1's position in the lane
F2's availability if D1 moves
A promise that the lane will clear

questions.explanation: The defender and teammate create the choice. A lane only becomes useful if it remains open after the movement.

questions.prompt: Arrange this shooting-lane read.

options.text: Identify D1 and F2
Check whether a lane or pass opens
Choose a shot, pass or protected touch

questions.explanation: Check the current lane and support, then choose among the available options. You do not have to wait for D1 to move.

questions.prompt: Move YOU sideways to change the shooting angle around D1.
questions.explanation: The example moves the carrier and puck sideways and changes the line to the net. Recheck D1, the goalie and F2; the position does not prove an open shot.

questions.prompt: D1 moves toward F2 and the direct lane opens. What deserves a new look?

options.text: Whether the open lane supports a shot or a pass now
Force a shot without checking the goalie or lane
Ignore F2 because D1 moved

questions.explanation: D1's movement changes the lane, but the carrier still reads space and support before choosing.

questions.prompt: How do your position and F2’s wider position offer different choices?
questions.explanation: YOU have a central shooting line with D1 in it; F2 offers a wider passing option. Compare those routes and explain what must stay open before using either.

scenarios.title: Guide the carrier to the wall
scenarios.objective: Use an inside angle to influence the carrier away from the middle without guessing the outcome.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks the left net (-x), defended by navy. F1 carries in a wide lane. YOU are closer to the middle, but F1 is closer to the left net than YOU. F2 trails across the middle. Work toward an inside approach while checking whether you can recover alongside the carrier.
cues: F1 is in a wide lane.
YOU are closer to the middle but farther from the left net than F1.
F2 trails on the other side of the middle.

sources.section: Limiting Opponent Options; Anticipation & Body Positioning
sources.use: Supports steering through position; no fixed distance or certain turnover.

questions.prompt: Where are YOU compared with wide F1?

options.text: Outside F1 toward the wall
Inside F1 toward the middle
Behind the goalie

questions.explanation: YOU are closer to the middle than F1, but that does not mean YOU are goal-side. F1 is currently closer to the left net.

questions.prompt: What does an inside approach try to preserve?

options.text: The middle and the route to the net
A chance to chase F2 wide immediately
A predictable carrier path regardless of movement

questions.explanation: An inside approach aims to protect the middle, but YOU still have to account for starting behind F1. A wall-side route or successful steering is not guaranteed; keep F2 in the scan.

questions.prompt: Arrange this angling read.

options.text: Find F1's route and the middle
Match the inside relationship
Update if F1 cuts back

questions.explanation: Angling is a relationship that must be updated when the carrier changes direction.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to F1 while staying on the side nearer the middle.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to F1 and remains nearer the middle. It still leaves YOU farther from the left net than F1, so recheck the recovery route rather than assuming the carrier is contained.

questions.prompt: F1 cuts back toward centre ice. What should you reassess?

options.text: Your inside relationship and the space F1 now wants
Continue toward the wall as if F1 stayed wide
Follow F2 instead of the carrier

questions.explanation: The cut-back changes F1's route and the inside gap. Re-match the carrier while protecting the middle.

questions.prompt: How could the middle and side boards guide your approach to F1?
questions.explanation: Try to preserve space toward the middle while reading F1’s route near the side boards. You begin behind the carrier; explain how that limits the approach and why F2 still matters.

scenarios.title: Backcheck the open runner
scenarios.objective: Choose a backcheck relationship for the uncovered attacker while a teammate pressures the puck.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks the left net (-x), defended by navy. In this rep, navy D1 is assigned to pressure gold F1, who owns the puck. Gold F2 trails across the middle. YOU start closer to the left net than F2 and must scan that runner while checking whether D1 can maintain pressure.
cues: D1 is assigned puck pressure; the freeze does not prove successful pressure.
F2 is a separate trailing gold attacker.
YOU start closer to the left net than F2, at the same up-ice coordinate as F1.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck-pressure assignment in this rep?

options.text: YOU
D1
F2

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns navy D1 to pressure gold F1. Whether D1 can stay with F1 remains part of the read.

questions.prompt: What belongs in your backcheck read?

options.text: F2’s route toward the left net
D1's ability to stay with F1
The puck alone, without scanning F2

questions.explanation: The uncovered runner toward the left net and D1’s pressure on F1 define the backcheck job.

questions.prompt: Arrange this backcheck check-in.

options.text: Find F2 and the left net
Skate into a useful relationship
Re-check F1, F2 and D1

questions.explanation: Look for a relationship that limits the runner’s passing or shooting options, then update as D1’s pressure changes.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward F2 while staying between F2 and the left net.
questions.explanation: This point closes the distance to F2 while staying on the net side of F2's route, without pretending that one spot solves the play.

questions.prompt: D1 cannot stay with F1 and calls for help. What should YOU reassess?

options.text: Whether to help pressure F1 while keeping track of F2
Leave both attackers to chase the puck
Stay on F2 without checking F1

questions.explanation: F1 is an opponent who may now need defensive pressure, not attacking support. Recheck both attackers and communicate with D1 before changing jobs.

questions.prompt: How is a backcheck different from simply skating toward the puck?
questions.explanation: It connects your route to an attacker and the net, so you can limit a pass or shot while reading the teammate pressure.

scenarios.title: Change jobs after the turnover
scenarios.objective: Switch from attacking support to defensive recovery when possession changes.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x). Gold D1 has won control, so gold now attacks the left net (-x). YOU and navy F1 must change from attacking support to defence. Gold F2 trails D1 on the other side of the middle.
cues: Gold D1 now owns the puck.
Gold F2 is a separate trailing option across the middle.

questions.prompt: What fact changes your earlier attacking plan?

options.text: D1 has won the puck
F2 is on the other side of the middle
YOU are closer to the left net than navy F1

questions.explanation: D1 is the new puck owner, so the possession relationship has changed.

questions.prompt: Which two cues shape your new defensive job?

options.text: D1's direction with the puck
F2's route toward the left net
The old support lane as if Navy still had possession

questions.explanation: The new carrier and second attacker set the recovery problem; the old attacking plan is stale.

questions.prompt: Put this turnover response in order.

options.text: Recognize D1 has possession
Find F2 and the left net
Choose a recovery relationship

questions.explanation: The job changes at the turnover, then the route is chosen from the new threat picture.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the defended left net, then recheck D1 and F2.
questions.explanation: The example moves YOU closer to the left net. D1 is still nearer that net than YOU; keep reading both gold attackers rather than assuming you have recovered ahead of the carrier.

questions.prompt: Navy F1 gains control back from D1 before gold F2 receives. What changes first?

options.text: Re-check possession and return to an attacking support read
Continue backchecking F2 without looking
Assume F2 still controls the puck

questions.explanation: F1 is your navy teammate. Confirm that regain and look for attacking support toward the right net, while checking gold pressure.

questions.prompt: How can one skater have two jobs within a few seconds?
questions.explanation: A turnover changes the puck carrier and direction. Explain how the same visible teammates require attacking support before the turnover and defensive recovery after it.
